cases.answerText: **42 inches minimum**, measured vertically from the bench’s uppermost surface—not the terrace walking surface—because the fixed bench is 12 inches horizontally from the guard, within the 21-inch threshold (BC § 1015.3). Separately, guards generally must prevent passage of a 4-inch sphere from the walking surface to the required guard height; between 36 and 42 inches, the stated limit is a 4⅜-inch sphere (BC § 1015.4). Guards must also resist a 50-pound-per-linear-foot load in accordance with ASCE 7 (BC § 1607.8.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText: No. At 20 inches above the walking surface, a 5-inch sphere may not pass through an opening in a required guard: the ordinary rule prohibits openings that allow a 4-inch sphere to pass from the walking surface up to the required guard height, and the stated exceptions do not apply (BC § 1015.4). Required guards are generally at least 42 inches high, measured from the adjacent walking surface (BC § 1015.3). The guard must also meet the applicable structural-load rule: a 50-pound-per-linear-foot load under the referenced standard; the supplied exception for certain areas not accessible to the general public does not fit the stated public terrace (BC § 1607.8.1).

cases.answerText: A 4-inch horizontal drainage pipe requires a minimum slope of **1/8 inch per foot**. Over 40 feet, that is a total fall of **5 inches** (40 × 1/8) (2022 NYC Plumbing Code § 704.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText: No. In a new NYC building, horizontal drainage pipes must have cleanouts at intervals **not more than 100 feet** apart; 120 feet exceeds that limit. The stated nonremovable-trap exception is limited to the section of horizontal fixture-drain piping between the trap and its vent connection, and does not authorize 120-foot spacing for ordinary horizontal sanitary drains (PC § 708.1.1).

cases.answerText: No. The 2022 NYC Plumbing Code requires each fixture trap to have a liquid seal at least 2 inches and not more than 4 inches deep, except that a deeper seal is allowed for special designs relating to accessible fixtures; a 1.5-inch seal is below the minimum (PC § 1002.4).

cases.answerText: No. The 2022 NYC Plumbing Code requires at least 15 inches from the water closet’s center to a side wall, partition, vanity, or other obstruction, so 14 inches is 1 inch short of that minimum (PC § 405.3.1). The separate minimum compartment width is 30 inches; it does not replace the center-to-side-wall clearance requirement.

cases.answerText: **Yes.** Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, the attic passageway exception permits a length of up to 50 feet if the passageway is unobstructed and at least 6 feet high and 24 inches wide throughout. The stated 30-foot length and dimensions meet those conditions for the length exception (MC § 306.3). This answers only the length condition, not overall installation approval.

cases.answerText: The minimum condensate pipe diameter is **1 inch**. For drains from multiple units manifolded together, MC § 307.2.2 directs sizing by Table 307.2.2; 30 tons falls in the “Over 20 tons to 40 tons” row. The section also requires condensate drain lines to be at least 3/4-inch internal diameter and not decrease in size from the drain-pan connection to disposal.

cases.answerText: Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, provide a **level working space at least 30 inches deep by 30 inches wide** in front of the appliance’s control side for servicing (MC § 306.1). The same section separately requires clearance as required by the NYC Electrical Code; that additional clearance is not specified in the supplied evidence.

cases.answerText: No. In a NYC garage, an appliance with an ignition source must have that source at least 18 inches above the floor; the exception is only for appliances listed as flammable-vapor-ignition resistant. Since you stipulated the heater is not so listed, a 12-inch height does not meet that requirement (2022 NYC FGC § 305.3; MC § 304.3).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText:
**Yes.** The NYC Mechanical Code requires a guard: the HVAC unit is within 10 feet of the roof edge, and the edge is more than 30 inches above the surface below (36 inches). The guard top must be at least **42 inches above the elevated surface adjacent to the guard** (MC § 304.11). It must also extend at least 30 inches beyond each end of the unit, prevent passage of a 21-inch-diameter sphere, and meet the NYC Building Code guard-loading requirements.

The Building Code generally sets a 42-inch minimum height for required guards (BC § 1015.3). Its guard-opening rule generally limits openings to a 4-inch sphere, with a 21-inch-sphere exception for elevated walking surfaces not open to the public that provide access to mechanical equipment (BC § 1015.4). The Mechanical Code’s stated 21-inch-sphere requirement applies here; whether the Building Code exception’s nonpublic-access condition also applies is not established. The Building Code also requires guards to resist a 50-plf linear load in accordance with ASCE 7; its one- and two-family dwelling exception refers to a separate concentrated-load requirement (BC § 1607.8.1; § 1607.8.1.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText: No. Under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code ordinary appliance rule, the shutoff valve must be in the same room and within 6 feet of the appliance; at 8 feet, it does not meet the distance limit. The rule also requires access, placement upstream of the union, connector, or quick-disconnect it serves, and a height no more than 60 inches above the finished floor. You stipulate that no exception applies. (FGC § 409.5.1)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText: **No—not under the supplied general rule.** FGC § 411.1, Item 2 permits a listed and labeled appliance connector up to 6 feet long, measured along its centerline, but says only one connector may be used per appliance; two 3-foot connectors cannot be joined under that rule. However, § 411.1 begins “Except as required by Section 411.1.1,” and that exception text is not supplied, so whether it changes the result for your appliance cannot be determined here.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText:
For gas distribution piping operating above 5 psig, the test pressure must be **at least twice the maximum allowable operating pressure (MAOP), and never less than 100 psig, for at least 1 hour** (FGC § 406.4.1, Exception 1). At 8 psig, that means a minimum of **100 psig for 1 hour**, assuming 8 psig is the MAOP; if the MAOP is higher than 50 psig, twice MAOP would exceed 100 psig. Measure the duration after the testing medium stabilizes. (FGC § 406.4.1.)

The code also requires piping to be gas-tight before service and inspected and pressure-tested before acceptance and initial operation. For gas distribution piping operating above 5 psig within buildings, all butt welds require radiographic testing under ASME BPVC Section IX. (FGC §§ 404.20, 406.1, 406.1.1.1.)

cases.label: incorrect_material
cases.note: Allows10-minute test;FGC406.4.2 requires30minutes. Independently confirmed official NYC PDF page19 (zero based).
cases.answerText: Yes—under the ordinary rule, a 10-minute test duration is enough, assuming no longer special test applies. FGC § 406.4.1 specifies minimum test pressures but does not set a general minimum duration; it requires duration to be measured after the testing medium stabilizes. Its stated exceptions require longer periods for gas piping above 5 psig (minimum 1 hour), piping in public corridors (minimum 30 minutes), and coated and wrapped pipe (minimum 60 minutes). Meter piping follows the serving utility’s testing requirements. Since you have excluded a longer special test, those exceptions do not change the ordinary-rule answer.

cases.answerText: **To the top of the pipe**, not its centerline. NYC FGC § 404.12 requires underground piping to be at least 24 inches below grade, measured to the pipe’s top. The steel-plate exception permits less burial depth only when its specified plate and installation conditions are met; you state there is no such plate, so that exception does not apply.

cases.answerText: **No.** The 2022 NYC Fire Code requires yards to be cleaned regularly to prevent accumulation of rubbish and other combustible waste; it does not make cleanup conditional on a fire or an exit obstruction. It also prohibits allowing rubbish or other combustible waste to accumulate on a premises (FC §§ 304.1, 304.1.1).

The 2022 NYC Fire Code states this baseline in FC 315.2.1. It separately allows the department to authorize noncombustible materials to be stored to the ceiling when the storage is within 30 inches (762 mm) of a fire partition; you stipulated that no department-authorized exception applies. citeresearch-permitext_discovered-id:31004696-1

cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText: **6 enclosed bicycle spaces.** For a residence in the table’s “all other types of residences” category, the requirement is 1 space per 2 dwelling units; 11 ÷ 2 = 5.5, and a fraction of 50% or greater counts as an additional space, giving 6. The table’s waiver for buildings or building segments containing 10 dwelling units or less does not apply to the stated 11-unit building. (ZR § 25-811)

cases.label: incorrect_minor
cases.note: Core requirement correct, but describes target8sf as an8sf reduction;15minus8is7.
cases.answerText: **No.** ZR 25-83 requires **15 square feet per bicycle space**; reducing that to 8 square feet requires the Buildings Commissioner to certify that the submitted layout adequately accommodates the specified number of bicycles. Without that certification, the 8-square-foot reduction is not authorized (ZR § 25-83).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText: **No.** For the ordinary off-site bicycle-parking option, ZR 25-84 permits the other zoning lot to be no farther than **1,000 feet** from the nearest boundary of the served lot. At **1,100 feet**, the room is outside that limit. The separate alternative for a subsurface parking and other service facility serving multiple zoning lots does not apply under your stated facts. (ZR § 25-84)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion matches frozen source key; no material contradictory addition identified.
cases.answerText: **No.** ZR 32-41 expressly allows accessory uses to be open or enclosed despite limitations on the principal use, provided any open accessory use is customarily found in connection with that principal use (ZR § 32-41). This is not an automatic prohibition on every outdoor accessory use; the customarily-found condition still applies. The supplied text also excepts provisions made specifically in permitted Use Groups and §§ 36-11 and 36-61. The supplied § 36-11 excerpt is incomplete, so whether it affects a particular application cannot be resolved from this packet.

cases.label: incorrect_material
cases.note: Denies ten-unit waiver expressly present in25-811;attributes waiver only to36-711.
cases.answerText: **No—not under ZR 25-811.** For the ordinary-residence category, that section’s table requires one bicycle-parking space per two dwelling units, so exactly 10 dwelling units yields a requirement of five spaces. ZR 36-711 separately states a waiver for buildings containing 10 dwelling units or less, but that waiver does not establish a waiver under ZR 25-811. The stipulated absence of a segment issue does not change this result.
